title: Object Storage vs File Storage vs Block Storage

blocks.text: Example: a photo app
Uploaded photos: use object storage. The app uploads and downloads each photo by its key, a name that identifies the object.
Shared editing folder: use file storage when several servers need the same files through normal file operations.
Database disk: use block storage for a database that needs frequent small reads and writes. The database manages its own records.
One system can use all three. Choose by how the application accesses and changes data.
Comparison

rows.html: Objects: data plus metadata, such as content type
A disk volume made of addressable blocks
Bucket + key, e.g. photos/42.jpg. A bucket contains objects.
Block address on a volume. A volume is a logical disk.
API calls, usually over HTTP: PUT, GET, DELETE
File operations: open, read, write. Network shares commonly use NFS or SMB.
Operating system reads and writes blocks. Usually a filesystem or database sits above it.
Usually replace the object. Some services support append or other updates.
Read or write part of a file; filesystem manages placement
Read or write selected blocks; upper layers manage files and records
Shared folders, existing apps that require file paths
Amazon EFS: a shared NFS filesystem
Amazon EBS: block volumes attached to compute instances

blocks.text: NFS (Network File System) and SMB (Server Message Block) are protocols for accessing files over a network.
Details that affect the choice
An S3 general purpose bucket has a flat key namespace. The slash in photos/42.jpg is part of the key; its folder display does not create normal filesystem directories.
A filesystem organizes files and directories on storage. Creating one on a block volume gives that server file paths, but does not automatically create a shared file service.
A network file share supports multiple clients. Applications still need locking or coordination when clients change the same file.
Some block volumes allow multiple servers to attach. Safe concurrent writes require a filesystem or application designed for shared block access.
Object update rules depend on the service. For example, S3 Express One Zone supports append in directory buckets. Check the API before assuming whole-object replacement is the only option.
Compare latency (time per operation), IOPS (operations per second), and throughput (bytes per second) for your workload. The storage type alone does not guarantee performance.
Compare total cost: stored capacity, requests, provisioned performance, retrieval, and data transfer. Rates and billing rules depend on the service.
